Area.evidence_source: International research consistently demonstrates reluctance on the part of young men to engage with health services, including in relation to mental health distress (Biddle, Gunnell, Sharp, & Donovan, 2004; Burke & McKeon, 2007; Centre for Suicide Prevention, 2007). Young men have been shown to be vulnerable to seeing mental distress and concomitant help seeking in negative terms (Barney, Griffiths, Jorm, & Christensen, 2006; Cleary, 2005; Stanistreet, Gabbay, Jeffrey, & Taylor, 2004). Consequently, they not only are less likely to disclose their own emotional distress but also are inhibited from accessing professional and/or lay support (Rickwood, Deane, & Wilson, 2007). These negative perceptions have been understood in three principal, overlapping ways. The first way is as a result of a cultural stigmatizing of mental illness (Burke & McKeon, 2007; Corrigan, 2005), on the basis of which those labeled as mentally ill are demeaned and marginalized. Responding to such cultural cues, young men are prompted to hide their own emotional distress as a means of avoiding deeply negative stereotyping and concomitant treatment by others. The second way is in terms of gender socialization, encompassing a number of related social processes that together work to uphold the 'male' attributes of emotional robustness and independence. Consequently, young men view help seeking for mental distress as implying weakness and vulnerability and, therefore, as something to be avoided (Gulliver, Griffiths, & Christensen, 2010). Finally, (young) men have been ascribed a relative lack of emotional competence and consequent poor recognition of personal mental distress, further inhibiting disclosure and help seeking (Möller-Leinkühler, 2002; Rickwood, Deane, Wilson, & Ciarrochi, 2005).
